about: ISSP Test Exam HS26 (Degen); built by notes/solid-state/build/testexam/build.py. Solutions are our own.

enc.title: Test exam HS26, Problem 1: multiple choice (4 pt)

source.where: Problem 1 (a)-(d), pages 2-3; solutions our own (no official key released)

questions.q: (a) What is the Miller index of the shaded lattice plane? (Axes: $x$ towards you, $y$ to the right, $z$ up; the plane passes through the hidden back-bottom-left corner, cuts the back-right vertical edge at $\frac12$ and the bottom-right edge at $\frac13$ from the back.)
questions.explain: The plane contains the origin, so shift it to $(0,1,0)$: intercepts $x=\frac13$, $y=-1$, $z=\frac12$. Reciprocals $(3,-1,2)$. Check: the normal of the plane through $(0,0,0),(0,1,\frac12),(\frac13,1,0)$ is $\propto(3,-1,2)$.

questions.q: (b) Normal modes of a diatomic linear chain (heavy atoms large, light atoms small): (a) nothing moves relative to anything (uniform translation, $k=0$); (b) heavy and light neighbours move against each other in every cell; (c) only the light atoms move, alternately, heavy ones at rest; (d) only the heavy atoms move, alternately, light ones at rest. Order by frequency.
questions.explain: (a) acoustic at $k=0$: $\omega=0$. (d) acoustic at the zone boundary: $\sqrt{2C/M}$. (c) optical at the zone boundary: $\sqrt{2C/m}$, larger since $m<M$. (b) optical at $k=0$: $\sqrt{2C(1/m+1/M)}$, the maximum.

questions.q: (c) Graphene (honeycomb lattice of carbon). Which statement about its phonon dispersion is correct?
options: The phonon branches are degenerate because of the hexagonal symmetry.
Graphene possesses both acoustic and optical phonons.
Being 2D, it has only two acoustic branches instead of three.
questions.explain: The honeycomb is a triangular Bravais lattice with a 2-atom basis: $3\cdot2=6$ branches, 3 acoustic (LA, TA and the out-of-plane flexural ZA) and 3 optical. Atoms move in 3D, so there are still three acoustic branches.

questions.q: (d) In the tight-binding model, the energy bands...
questions.explain: Bandwidth $\propto$ overlap integral. Higher atomic levels have more extended orbitals, so neighbouring orbitals overlap more and the bands get wider (and may then overlap; low-lying core bands are nearly flat).

enc.title: Test exam boss: crystallography of the FCC lattice (10 pt)

source.where: Problem 2 (a)-(d), pages 4-7; solutions our own (no official key released)

enc.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (the test exam had about 1 point per 3 minutes). Then enter the numbers.
statement: FCC unit cell (cube of side $a$, atoms at the corners and face centres).
(a) (1 pt) Starting from a simple cubic Bravais lattice with side $a$, write the 4-point basis that generates FCC.

(b) (3 pt) The structure factor is $F(\mathbf q)=\sum_jf_j(\mathbf q)\,e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_j}$. Find $F$ for the monatomic FCC crystal (form factor $f$) and the conditions on the Miller indices for an observable peak.

(c) (4 pt) TEM electron diffraction shows a projection of the reciprocal lattice onto the plane perpendicular to the beam. Beam along $\hat z$ (only $h,k$ non-zero). i. Sketch the pattern and label at least two spots. ii. Can this pattern alone tell FCC from BCC or simple cubic? iii. From which direction of incidence would you expect a hexagonal pattern?

(d) (2 pt) Small angles: find the interplanar spacing $d$ from the wavelength $\lambda$, the distance $R$ between direct and diffracted spot on the detector, and the camera length $L$. Game numbers (not in the exam): $\lambda=2.51$ pm (200 keV electrons), $L=1.00$ m, $R=12.0$ mm.

finalAnswers.prompt: (c) In the $[001]$ pattern, distance of the $(220)$ spot from the centre divided by that of $(200)$.
(d) $d$ in nm for the game numbers.

keyPoints: (a) Basis $\mathbf r_1=0$, $\mathbf r_2=\frac a2(1,1,0)$, $\mathbf r_3=\frac a2(1,0,1)$, $\mathbf r_4=\frac a2(0,1,1)$ on the simple cubic lattice $a(n_1,n_2,n_3)$.

(b) With $\mathbf q=\mathbf G_{hkl}=\frac{2\pi}a(h,k,l)$: $F=f\left[1+e^{i\pi(h+k)}+e^{i\pi(h+l)}+e^{i\pi(k+l)}\right]$. $F=4f$ if $h,k,l$ are all even or all odd, $F=0$ if mixed. First peaks: $(111),(200),(220),(311),(222)$.

(c) i. Beam along $z$: spots $(hk0)$ with $h,k$ both even (since $l=0$ is even): a square grid $(200),(020),(\bar200),(0\bar20)$ at distance $\frac{4\pi}a$ and $(220)$-type on the diagonals at $\sqrt2$ times that.

(c) ii. No: simple cubic [001] gives a square grid of $(100)$-type spots, BCC gives a square grid of $(110)$/$(200)$ spots rotated by $45^\circ$, FCC a square grid of $(200)$/$(220)$. All are square; without knowing $a$ (absolute spacing) they cannot be told apart from this one pattern.
(c) iii. Along a body diagonal, $[111]$: the reciprocal lattice points perpendicular to it ($(2\bar20)$, $(20\bar2)$, $(02\bar2)$, ...) form a triangular net with sixfold symmetry.
(d) $\tan2\theta=R/L\approx2\theta$ and Bragg $\lambda=2d\sin\theta\approx2d\theta$: $d=\frac{\lambda L}{R}$. Game numbers: $d=2.51\,{\rm pm}\cdot1\,{\rm m}/12\,{\rm mm}=0.209$ nm.

enc.title: Test exam boss: electronic and thermal properties of silver (5 pt)

source.where: Problem 3 (a)-(d), pages 8-11; solutions our own (no official key released), numbers checked in build.py

enc.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (hand calculator only, as in the exam). Enter at least 3 significant digits.
statement: Silver: free-electron model (nearly spherical Fermi surface), one valence electron per atom, mass density $10.5\ {\rm g/cm^3}$, atomic mass $107.8$ u.
(a) (1 pt) Electron density of the valence electrons.
(b) (2 pt) Radius of the Fermi surface in $\text{Å}^{-1}$.
(c) (1 pt) Fermi energy and Fermi temperature (in K).
(d) (1 pt) The melting point is $T_m=1235$ K $\ll T_F$. Why is there no significant heat exchange from these “hot” electrons to the lattice?
keyPoints: (b) Two spin states per $k$-point: $n=\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2}$, so $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}=1.20\times10^{10}\ {\rm m^{-1}}=1.20\ \text{Å}^{-1}$.

(d) Pauli principle: an electron deep in the Fermi sea cannot lose energy, because all states below it are occupied. Only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $E_F$ can exchange energy with the lattice; the electron gas is in equilibrium at the lattice temperature $T$, not at $T_F$.
(d) Consequence: electronic heat capacity $C_e=\frac{\pi^2}2Nk_B\frac T{T_F}$, only about $T/T_F\approx2\%$ of the classical value even at the melting point.
